03 Mood and cognition · class card

Lithium and anticonvulsants

lithium · valproate · carbamazepine · oxcarbazepine · lamotrigine · topiramate

Key point
  • Lithium: a narrow window (0.6 to 1.2 mEq/L), cleared by the kidneys; its levels, toxicity and interactions sit on its own brief
  • Any rash on lamotrigine: stop it; valproate raises its level and rash risk; after a sudden stop, restart at the starting dose
  • Valproate: check ammonia when confused and lipase with epigastric pain (pancreatitis: stop it); liver tests at the start and throughout; neural tube defects in pregnancy
  • Carbamazepine: in Asian ancestry, screen for human leukocyte antigen (HLA) B*1502 before starting; follow the CBC and sodium; it induces liver enzymes, so a contraceptive pill can fail
Drugs

Lithium Lithobid (lithium carbonate)

Valproate (valproic acid; divalproex Depakote)

Carbamazepine Tegretol Equetro

Oxcarbazepine Trileptal

Lamotrigine Lamictal

Topiramate Topamax

The anticonvulsants that stabilize mood: valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine ("Valentine Cards are Lame")

Mechanism

Lithium: how it calms mania is unknown; the kidneys clear nearly all of it avoided in kidney disease

Valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine: block voltage-gated sodium channels neurons fire less

Valproate: inhibits gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) transaminase more GABA

Carbamazepine: liver enzymes induced (cytochrome P450 3A4), its own metabolism included levels typically stabilize at 2 to 4 weeks

Topiramate: more GABA action sedation and fatigue

Uses

Lithium: acute treatment and maintenance in bipolar disorder

Valproate: mania, acute and maintenance; also seizures and migraine prevention

Carbamazepine: acute mania; seizures; trigeminal neuralgia (first line, with oxcarbazepine)

Lamotrigine: maintenance and bipolar depression, not acute mania Lamotrigine"Relapsigine": lamotrigine prevents relapse.

Oxcarbazepine: matches carbamazepine for mood with fewer adverse effects, including less rash and less liver toxicity

Topiramate: prevents migraine and treats binge eating disorder; it has shown no benefit in bipolar disorder

Adverse effects

Lithium: tremor, nystagmus, polyuria and thirst, hypothyroidism, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, or arginine vasopressin resistance (nephrogenic) Nephrogenic diabetes insipidusLithium builds up in collecting duct cells and blocks the action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH), so free water is lost.

Valproate: GI upset (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), weight gain, sedation, tremor, ataxia, hair loss ValproateHair loss in 5% to 10%. Hyperandrogenism in women; it may raise the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome.

Valproate, rare but serious: hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, hyperammonemic encephalopathy, thrombocytopenia HyperammonemiaA valproate metabolite, propionic acid, stops the urea cycle clearing ammonia; liver failure or a urea cycle disorder is a reason not to use it.

Carbamazepine: sleepiness, nausea, diarrhea, rash; double vision (diplopia), ataxia CarbamazepineVitamin D deficiency may occur: the induced enzyme breaks vitamin D down.

Carbamazepine, serious: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), agranulocytosis, aplastic anemia, low sodium, liver toxicity

Oxcarbazepine: fatigue, dizziness, somnolence, double vision; hyponatremia OxcarbazepineAbout 25% to 30% of patients with a carbamazepine hypersensitivity reaction react to oxcarbazepine too (label).

Lamotrigine: the most common effects are nausea, dizziness, fatigue, insomnia; up to 10% get a benign rash; SJS or TEN in about 0.1% Lamotrigine labelThe label also warns of aseptic meningitis.

Topiramate: weight loss, kidney stones, sedation, cognitive slowing, speech dysfunction; myopia with acute angle-closure glaucoma; metabolic acidosis Topiramate labelThe acidosis is hyperchloremic, with a normal anion gap. Decreased sweating (oligohidrosis) is reported.

Other

Pregnancy, valproate: neural tube defects and other major malformations Valproate in pregnancyAlso oral clefts, heart and urogenital malformations; in childhood, cognitive deficits, autism and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder.

Pregnancy, carbamazepine: neural tube, heart and craniofacial defects

Pregnancy, lithium: Ebstein anomaly and other heart defects

Pregnancy, topiramate: cleft lip or palate; lamotrigine: relatively safe PregnancyUse in the first trimester may raise the risk of oral clefts slightly. Topiramate can also leave the baby small for gestational age.

Rash on lamotrigineA benign rash and early SJS or TEN cannot be told apart

Risk is higher in children, with valproate, or with a fast titration

If a rash of any kind appears on lamotrigine, choose stopping lamotrigine and switching to another agent.

DRESS (drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms)A polymorphic rash, typically with liver or other organ involvement, 2 to 8 weeks into carbamazepine or lamotrigine

Eosinophilia is often present (lamotrigine label) Lamotrigine skinSJS is the most serious skin reaction on lamotrigine.

If DRESS appears, choose stopping the drug.

Valproate pancreatitisEpigastric pain and vomiting with a raised lipase; idiosyncratic, so dose and years on the drug do not rule it out

In most cases it resolves after the cause is removed

If acute pancreatitis appears on valproate, choose stopping valproate.

Confusion on valproateDrowsiness or confusion on valproate: a metabolite blocks the urea cycle

Once the diagnosis is confirmed: stop valproate and look for an underlying urea cycle disorder

If confusion develops on valproate, choose checking plasma ammonia.

Valproate toxicity with GI symptomsVomiting, diarrhea and confusion on valproate

If GI symptoms and altered mental status appear on valproate and the question asks which result is abnormal, choose liver function tests, which are likely abnormal with a high ammonia.

Carbamazepine blood dyscrasiaAgranulocytosis or aplastic anemia, typically in the first 3 to 4 months

Clozapine also causes agranulocytosis

If a blood dyscrasia appears on carbamazepine, choose stopping carbamazepine; some of these recover after the stop.

Carbamazepine in Asian ancestryAn allele typical of Asian ancestry carries the SJS and TEN risk on carbamazepine

If carbamazepine is planned in a patient of Asian ancestry, choose HLA-B*1502 testing first, and avoiding the drug if the allele is present.

Low sodium on carbamazepine or oxcarbazepineConfusion with a low sodium: syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH), dose-dependent, on carbamazepine; hyponatremia on oxcarbazepine

If the hyponatremia is symptomatic, choose considering a stop of carbamazepine; with oxcarbazepine, some patients need a lower dose, a stop or fluid limits.

Carbamazepine overdoseSodium channel block can widen the QRS Carbamazepine overdoseAnticholinergic effects (hyperthermia, flushed skin, dilated pupils), tachycardia and hypotension. Care is mainly supportive.

Levels are repeated until they fall: the peak can take days

If the QRS is wide or the rhythm is abnormal, choose sodium bicarbonate; continuous cardiac monitoring may be needed.

Valproate overdoseLethargy; anion gap metabolic acidosis, hypernatremia, hypocalcemia, high ammonia Valproate overdoseGlucose, acetaminophen and salicylate levels, and an electrocardiogram; in severe cases sodium, bicarbonate, calcium, ammonia, platelets and liver tests.

Hemodialysis may remove much of the drug in overdose

If a valproate overdose is suspected, choose valproate levels every 2 to 3 hours, since a delayed-release tablet can peak late.

Interactions, by result
Combined withResultRule
Valproate added to lamotrigineLamotrigine level more than doubles; rash risk risesLower lamotrigine dose, slower titration
Carbamazepine with lamotrigineLamotrigine level fallsA higher lamotrigine dose may be needed
Carbamazepine with an oral contraceptiveThe pill is cleared faster (enzyme induction)It can fail: unplanned pregnancy
Carbamazepine or an estrogen pill, with valproateFaster valproate clearanceIts level falls
An estrogen pill, with lamotrigineLamotrigine is cleared fasterLower level; it may climb again in the hormone-free week
Low albumin, with valproateMore unbound valproateToxicity even at usual doses
A thiazide, a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug or an ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor, with lithiumLess lithium cleared by the kidneys Level rises: toxicity
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Valproate, at the start and throughoutDrug level (target 50 to 125 mcg/mL), liver tests, CBC with plateletsDose-related toxicity and rare serious adverse effects (timing in the chart)
Carbamazepine, before the first doseHLA-B*1502 if of Asian ancestryRisk of a serious skin reaction
Carbamazepine, duringLevel at 5 days (steady state) and again a few weeks on; CBC, sodium, liver testsSelf-induction changes how the drug is handled early on; plus its serious adverse effects
Oxcarbazepine, during maintenanceSodium, consideredA known adverse effect of oxcarbazepine in about 2.5%
LamotrigineBaseline CBC, liver tests and basic metabolic panel; then none, and no levelsDoses are set by the clinical response
Topiramate, at baseline and periodicallySerum bicarbonateA label warning about an acid-base effect
Where the choice is made

Which mood stabilizer for which patient, and in pregnancy

Lithium levels, toxicity and its treatment, interactions, nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism

Topiramate for binge eating

Clozapine and its agranulocytosis

How NBME framed it

Setup A mood stabilizer for years at a steady dose and light drinking; now epigastric pain and vomiting

Offered alcohol, ibuprofen

Deciding the pancreatitis is idiosyncratic: neither the dose nor the years on it matter; under 14 drinks a week makes alcohol unlikely, and ibuprofen is not typically a cause

Answer valproic acid

Setup Vomiting, loose stools and slowed thinking on valproate

Offered serum creatinine, leukocyte count

Deciding GI symptoms with altered mental status on valproate point to its toxicity; creatinine is generally unaffected by valproate

Answer liver function tests

Setup On lithium, a tremor that spills a cup, with diarrhea and ataxia, days after a drug was added

Offered omeprazole, lovastatin

Deciding only one added drug changes how the kidney handles sodium, and lithium follows sodium back into the blood

Answer hydrochlorothiazide

Setup Decades on lithium; confused and unsteady, with a high sodium and dilute urine

Offered acute lithium toxicity, lithium hypothyroidism, routine lithium effects

Deciding hypernatremia with inappropriately dilute urine; a mildly raised thyroid-stimulating hormone does not explain it

Answer nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

Practice
  1. 27-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder, 3 weeks into lamotrigine a few itchy pink macules on her chest since yesterday no fever, blisters or mouth sores; feels well T 37.0 °C · HR 78/min → Stop lamotrigine → any rash on lamotrigine means stopping it, because a benign rash and early Stevens-Johnson syndrome cannot be told apart; continuing at the same or a lower dose is the trap
  2. 45-year-old man with bipolar I disorder on valproate for 4 months family reports 2 days of drowsiness and confusion no abdominal pain; no jaundice; no new drugs valproate level in range · AST and ALT normal → Plasma ammonia → confusion on valproate calls for an ammonia level: a valproate metabolite blocks ammonia elimination in the urea cycle; lipase is for epigastric pain, and the platelet count tracks thrombocytopenia
  3. 34-year-old woman on valproate for bipolar I disorder for 3 years a day of epigastric pain boring to the back, with vomiting one glass of wine weekly; no gallstones on ultrasound lipase 6 times the upper limit of normal → Stop valproate → valproate pancreatitis is idiosyncratic, unrelated to dose or duration, and in most cases resolves once the drug is stopped; years on a stable dose do not exclude it
  4. 31-year-old man of Asian ancestry with bipolar I disorder carbamazepine planned for mania after lithium and valproate were not tolerated no drug allergies; liver tests and CBC normal sodium 139 mEq/L → HLA-B*1502 testing → before carbamazepine in a patient of Asian ancestry, screen for HLA-B*1502 and avoid the drug if it is present, because of Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis; levels come after steady state, and ammonia belongs to valproate
  5. 24-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder has a positive pregnancy test started carbamazepine 4 months ago takes a combined estrogen-progestin pill daily no missed pills, no vomiting, no other drugs → Induction of liver enzymes → carbamazepine induces cytochrome P450 enzymes, which clear the oral contraceptive faster and can end in an unplanned pregnancy; enzyme inhibition is how valproate raises lamotrigine, and protein binding matters for valproate when albumin is low
  6. 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, stable on lamotrigine for a year now in a manic episode; valproate is being added no rash; liver tests, CBC and sodium normal BP 122/78 mm Hg · HR 84/min → Lower the lamotrigine dose → valproate inhibits lamotrigine clearance, raising its level and the rash risk, so the lamotrigine dose comes down and titration slows; lamotrigine levels are not needed, because dosing follows the clinical response
  7. 29-year-old man with bipolar II disorder stopped lamotrigine 3 weeks ago had taken a stable dose for a year; ran out while traveling mood now low; wants to restart; never had a rash → Restart at the starting dose and titrate up → after lamotrigine is stopped suddenly, it restarts at the initial dose with titration rather than at the old dose, since rapid dose escalation raises the rash risk; levels are not needed
  8. 52-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, confused for 2 days carbamazepine dose raised 3 weeks ago no vomiting, diarrhea or diuretics; no rash sodium 124 mEq/L · ammonia normal · AST and ALT normal → Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone → carbamazepine carries a dose-dependent risk of SIADH and hyponatremia; hyperammonemic encephalopathy belongs to valproate, and DRESS typically brings a rash with organ involvement 2 to 8 weeks in
  9. 38-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder, on valproate for 2 months 3 days: vomiting, loose stools, poor appetite slow to answer; disoriented to the date Vital signs normal · takes no other medications → Liver function tests → gastrointestinal symptoms with altered mental status on valproate point to its toxicity, with abnormal liver tests and hyperammonemia; valproate generally does not affect creatinine, and a low leukocyte count would not explain the gastrointestinal symptoms and the confusion
